t: Design a 3D Binary Matrix with Efficient Layer Tracking
o: Support set/unset of single cells and query the layer x with the most 1's (ties → largest x). With n ≤ 100, even rescanning all n layer counts per query is only 10^4 · 100 = 10^6 operations — perfectly fine. For larger scales, a max-heap of (count, x) snapshots with lazy deletion answers queries in O(log) amortized.
k: Only per-layer counts matter; cell coordinates (y, z) are irrelevant beyond incrementing/decrementing count[x].
Linear-scan query: iterate x from n−1 down with strict '>' comparison so ties naturally resolve to the largest index.
Heap approach: push (−count, x) on every increment; an entry is valid iff its snapshot equals the current count; pop invalid tops before answering.

a.i: Maintain cnt[x]; largestMatrix scans all layers from the top, keeping the first (largest) maximum.
s: largestMatrix: scan x = n−1…0, return the first x achieving the maximum
a.t: O(1) per update, O(n) per query — 10^4 · 100 = 10^6 total, well within limits

a.i: Push (−count, x) whenever a layer's count grows. Stale entries (snapshot ≠ current count) are discarded lazily at query time; the top valid entry is the answer because the true maximum layer always has an entry matching its current count.
s: largestMatrix: pop heap tops whose snapshot mismatches cnt, then return the top's x (fallback n−1 if the heap empties)
a.t: O(log) amortized per update/query — each pushed entry is popped at most once
a.sp: O(number of setCell calls) for heap entries

w: For the given constraints the linear scan is the pragmatic choice; mention the heap to show scalability awareness (it matters if n were 10^5+). Tie-breaking is the main bug source: scanning downward with strict '>' or encoding x negatively in the heap both handle 'largest x wins'. Edge case: all-zero matrix must return n−1.
